items.title: Courting Controversy: Privacy Law, Press Blind Spot
items.summary: In 1972, five men were caught breaking into the offices of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex in Washington, DC. What looked like a petty burglary to most, was not considered to be so by two reporters at The Washington Post, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein. Over the next two years, through late-night phone calls, doorstepping reluctant officials and clandestine meetings, they traced the break-in back to President Richard Nixon’s re-election campaign and, eventually, to the White House itself. Their reporting helped unravel the scandal that forced Nixon to resign in August 1974. Their account of it was made into a film called All the President’s Men , which took its title from Nixon’s aides whose names, money trails and private dealings were painstakingly exposed by the reporters. Now imagine Woodward and Bernstein, before writing a single word, sending a polite note to each of Nixon’s men seeking consent to process their personal data. Imagine, too, the presses grinding to a halt the moment one of them withdrew that consent and demanded that his data be erased. items.title: Arbitrary power thrives on ignorance, fear: Supreme Court Justice Ujjal Bhuyan
items.summary: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan on Saturday said that scientific temper lays the foundation for the rule of law, since arbitrary power feeds on a society that does not question. "I believe, scientific temperament lays the foundation for the rule of law. This is because arbitrary power thrives on ignorance, fear and unexamined belief," he said. Justice Bhuyan was delivering the address at the 12th convocation ceremony of the University of Science and Technology Meghalaya (USTM). He went on to set out what happens to a society that stops asking questions. "A society that accepts claims without evidence is susceptible to superstitious beliefs and becomes vulnerable to mis-information. A society that fears questions becomes vulnerable to authoritarianism. A society that treats tradition as beyond scrutiny may fail to reform unjust practices," he said. Referring to Article 51A of the Constitution, which makes developing a scientific temper a fundamental duty of every citizen, the judge said one need not be a scientist to develop it. items.title: A Fundamental Right
items.summary: With its new law that makes education a fundamental right with effect from April 1, 2010, India joins a small group of countries with such a statutory provision. All children in the 6 to 14 age group can exercise the right under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. An estimated one crore children who do not go to school now are expected to benefit.

items.title: COP17 adopts Yerevan Pathway as countries struggle to meet global biodiversity targets
items.summary: The 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) concluded in Yerevan, Armenia, on October 31, with countries adopting a new roadmap to accelerate global action on biodiversity. The conference's central challenge, however, remains unresolved, as countries have fallen behind on their commitments to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030, with only four years left to meet the targets. The two-week conference adopted nearly 50 decisions, including the Yerevan Pathway, a negotiated response to the first global review of collective progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). The framework, adopted in 2022, set out 23 targets to be achieved by 2030, including conserving 30% of the world's land and seas, restoring degraded ecosystems, and mobilising resources for biodiversity protection. The first global review of KMGBF, informed by the “State of Biodiversity Action” report released ahead of the conference, found that collective efforts are insufficient to achieve KMGBF’s targets within the stipulated timeframe.
